--- lecture: "13b" metadata-files: - ../../_slide-settings.yml format: revealjs: theme: default --- ::: {.my-title} # [Foundations of]{.my-subtitle}
[Data Science]{.blue} ::: {.my-grey} [{{< meta semester >}} | {{< meta course >}}]{}
[Jeffrey M. Girard | Lecture {{< meta lecture >}}]{} ::: ![](../../img/proud_coder_357EDD.svg){.absolute bottom=30 right=0 width="400"} ::: ## Roadmap ::: {.columns .pv4} ::: {.column width="60%"} - Extract and draw polygon map data in ggplot2 - Add points and text labels to existing maps - Join data with map data and make complex maps ::: ::: {.column .tc .pv4 width="40%"} {{< lif "../../icons/map.json" trigger=hover colors=secondary:#2a76dd class=rc >}} ::: ::: # Drawing Maps ## Where Do Maps Come From? {.fsmaller} ::: {.columns .pv4} ::: {.column width="60%"} - To draw a map, we need a dataset of geographic coordinates - These coordinates define the boundary lines of countries, states, or counties - The `map_data()` function from the \{maps\} package provides easy access - It returns a data frame of longitude and latitude points - We will then plot the region shapes using `geom_polygon()` ::: ::: {.column .tc .pv4 width="40%"} {{< lif "../../icons/globe.json" trigger=hover colors=secondary:#2a76dd class=rc >}} ::: ::: ## Extracting State Data ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) library(maps) # Extract the coordinates for the kansas map kansas <- map_data("county", "kansas") |> as_tibble() |> print(n = 5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 997 × 6 long lat group order region subregion 1 -95.1 37.7 1 1 kansas allen 2 -95.5 37.7 1 2 kansas allen 3 -95.5 37.7 1 3 kansas allen 4 -95.5 38.0 1 4 kansas allen 5 -95.1 38.0 1 5 kansas allen # ℹ 992 more rows ``` ::: ::: ## Understanding Map Data - **long** and **lat**: The x and y coordinates of the boundary lines - **group**: A unique identifier for each polygon (e.g., a specific island or continuous landmass) - **order**: The sequence in which the points should be connected to draw the shape correctly - **region**: The name of the geographic area (e.g., state) - **subregion:** The name of the area portion (e.g., county) ## Drawing Polygons ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(kansas, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group)) + geom_polygon(fill = "white", color = "black") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](b_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){width=1152} ::: ::: ## Fixing the Distortion ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(kansas, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group)) + geom_polygon(fill = "white", color = "black") + coord_quickmap() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](b_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=1152} ::: ::: # Wrangling Map Data ## Pulling All States ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Extract the coordinates for all US states state_map <- map_data("state") |> as_tibble() |> print(n = 10) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 15,537 × 6 long lat group order region subregion 1 -87.5 30.4 1 1 alabama 2 -87.5 30.4 1 2 alabama 3 -87.5 30.4 1 3 alabama 4 -87.5 30.3 1 4 alabama 5 -87.6 30.3 1 5 alabama 6 -87.6 30.3 1 6 alabama 7 -87.6 30.3 1 7 alabama 8 -87.6 30.3 1 8 alabama 9 -87.7 30.3 1 9 alabama 10 -87.8 30.3 1 10 alabama # ℹ 15,527 more rows ``` ::: ::: ## Drawing the US Map ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(state_map, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group)) + geom_polygon(fill = "steelblue", color = "black", linewidth = 0.5) + coord_quickmap() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](b_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=1152} ::: ::: ## Filtering Regions ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # We can use standard dplyr tools to map specific regions midwest_map <- state_map |> filter(region %in% c("kansas", "missouri", "iowa", "nebraska")) ggplot(midwest_map, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group)) + geom_polygon(fill = "wheat", color = "black") + coord_quickmap() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](b_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){width=1152} ::: ::: # Points and Labels ## Overlaying Data {.fsmaller} ::: {.columns .pv4} ::: {.column width="60%"} - Maps are most useful when they provide context for other data - Because maps in ggplot2 are just standard geoms, we can easily layer other geoms on top of them - `geom_point()` is great for cities, events, or locations - `geom_text()` or `geom_label()` can identify specific places ::: ::: {.column .tc .pv4 width="40%"} {{< lif "../../icons/translate.json" trigger=hover colors=secondary:#2a76dd class=rc >}} ::: ::: ## A City Dataset ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Let's create a small dataset of cities cities <- tribble( ~city, ~long, ~lat, "Lawrence", -95.2353, 38.9717, "St. Louis", -90.1994, 38.6270, "Des Moines", -93.6091, 41.5868, "Omaha", -95.9345, 41.2565 ) cities ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 4 × 3 city long lat 1 Lawrence -95.2 39.0 2 St. Louis -90.2 38.6 3 Des Moines -93.6 41.6 4 Omaha -95.9 41.3 ``` ::: ::: ## Separating Aesthetics ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} p_midwest <- ggplot() + geom_polygon( data = midwest_map, mapping = aes( x = long, y = lat, group = group ), fill = "white", color = "black" ) + coord_quickmap() p_midwest ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](b_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){width=864} ::: ::: ## Adding Points ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} p_midwest + geom_point( data = cities, aes(x = long, y = lat), color = "red", size = 4 ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](b_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){width=864} ::: ::: ## Adding Labels ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} p_midwest + geom_point( data = cities, aes(x = long, y = lat), color = "red", size = 3 ) + geom_text( data = cities, aes( x = long, y = lat, label = city ), nudge_y = 0.3, # shift up fontface = "bold" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](b_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=864} ::: ::: # Choropleth Maps ## What is a Choropleth? {.fsmaller} ::: {.columns .pv4} ::: {.column width="60%"} - A **choropleth map** uses color or shading to represent statistical data across geographic regions - For example, coloring states based on their population density or average temperature - To create one, we must merge our geographic polygon data with our statistical data using a join ::: ::: {.column .tc .pv4 width="40%"} {{< lif "../../icons/crayons.json" trigger=hover colors=secondary:#2a76dd class=rc >}} ::: ::: ## Preparing Statistical Data ::: {.cell replace_path='["../../data/",""]'} ```{.r .cell-code} arrests <- read_csv("arrests.csv") arrests ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 50 × 5 region Murder Assault UrbanPop Rape 1 alabama 13.2 236 58 21.2 2 alaska 10 263 48 44.5 3 arizona 8.1 294 80 31 4 arkansas 8.8 190 50 19.5 5 california 9 276 91 40.6 6 colorado 7.9 204 78 38.7 # ℹ 44 more rows ``` ::: ::: ## Joining the Data ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # We use left_join() to attach the statistics to the map boundaries state_joined <- state_map |> left_join(arrests, by = "region") state_joined ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 15,537 × 10 long lat group order region subregion Murder Assault UrbanPop Rape 1 -87.5 30.4 1 1 alabama 13.2 236 58 21.2 2 -87.5 30.4 1 2 alabama 13.2 236 58 21.2 3 -87.5 30.4 1 3 alabama 13.2 236 58 21.2 4 -87.5 30.3 1 4 alabama 13.2 236 58 21.2 5 -87.6 30.3 1 5 alabama 13.2 236 58 21.2 6 -87.6 30.3 1 6 alabama 13.2 236 58 21.2 # ℹ 15,531 more rows ``` ::: ::: ## Creating the Choropleth ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # We map the fill aesthetic to one of our statistical variables ggplot(state_joined, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group)) + geom_polygon(aes(fill = Murder), color = "white", linewidth = 0.3) + coord_quickmap() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](b_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){width=1152} ::: ::: ## Polishing the Map ::: {.cell output-location='slide'} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot( state_joined, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group) ) + geom_polygon( aes(fill = Murder), color = "white", linewidth = 0.3 ) + coord_quickmap() + scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma") + # use better colors theme_void() + # remove the axes and gridlines labs( title = "US Murder Arrest Rates", fill = "Rate per 100k" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](b_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){width=1152} ::: ::: ## Summary - **Coordinates:** Alter how space is mapped using `coord_fixed()`, `coord_polar()`, and `coord_quickmap()` - **Polygons:** Build basic maps using `map_data()` and `geom_polygon()`, ensuring `group` is mapped properly - **Layers:** Add context to maps by layering `geom_point()` and `geom_text()` from separate data sources - **Choropleths:** Color geographic regions by joining statistical data to spatial boundary data

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
